title: Session Hosts and Golden Images: Sizing, Building, and Versioning
monthTitle: Azure Virtual Desktop Infrastructure: Plan, Deploy & Scale
summary: This lesson covers the two things that determine whether your session hosts are fast, secure, and maintainable: how you size the VM, and how you build and version the image it boots from. You'll learn to size VMs by workload class, choose between Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session and single-session editions, build a golden image the right way, version it through Azure Compute Gallery, automate the build with Azure Image Builder, and make informed choices about Trusted Launch and disk type.
objectives: Size session host VM SKUs appropriately for light, medium, and heavy workload classes
Choose between Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session and single-session editions for a given host pool type
Describe the golden image workflow and why you build once and version rather than patch every host individually
Explain how Azure Compute Gallery versions and replicates images for use across host pools and regions
Explain what Azure Image Builder automates and when to use it instead of a manual golden image process
Decide between Trusted Launch and standard VMs, and between ephemeral and managed OS disks, for a given scenario

quiz.q: A pooled host pool runs Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session for general office productivity users, roughly 6 users per host. Which sizing approach is correct?
options: Size the VM's vCPU, memory, and disk IOPS around the expected concurrent session count and workload class (light/medium/heavy), then validate with a pilot before committing to the fleet-wide SKU
Pick the cheapest available SKU regardless of vCPU-to-user ratio, since AVD automatically compensates for undersized VMs
Always use GPU-enabled VM SKUs for any multi-session pooled host pool
Match the VM size to the single heaviest individual user's laptop specification
quiz.why: There's no single 'correct' SKU — sizing is a function of concurrent sessions per host and the workload class those sessions represent (light task work vs. heavy engineering/design work). The practical approach is to size against Microsoft's workload-class guidance and your expected density, then validate against a real pilot before locking in the fleet-wide VM size.

quiz.q: Why would a pooled host pool use Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session instead of a standard single-session edition?
options: Multi-session is required for FSLogix to function at all
Multi-session allows several concurrent users to share one VM's Windows OS instance, improving compute density and cost efficiency for shared, non-persistent pooled desktops
Multi-session is only available for personal host pools
Multi-session removes the need for a host pool entirely
quiz.why: Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session is licensed and engineered specifically to let multiple users run concurrent interactive sessions on the same VM, which is what makes pooled host pools cost-efficient at scale. Personal host pools, by contrast, typically use single-session editions since each VM is dedicated to one user.

quiz.q: What is the core benefit of the 'golden image' approach compared to configuring each session host individually after deployment?
options: It removes the need for any patching after deployment forever
It is required by Microsoft licensing for all host pools

You build and validate the OS, applications, and configuration once, then roll that consistent, tested image out to every new or replaced session host — eliminating configuration drift and manual per-host setup
It automatically enables RDP Shortpath
quiz.why: The golden image approach bakes the OS, apps, agents, and configuration into a single tested artifact. Every session host — new or replaced — boots from that same consistent image, eliminating drift between hosts and manual configuration work that would otherwise happen one machine at a time.

quiz.q: What role does Azure Compute Gallery play in the golden image workflow?
options: It replaces the need for Azure Image Builder
It is only used for marketplace images, not custom images
It automatically patches running session hosts in place
It stores, versions, and replicates your image definitions across regions and subscriptions, so session host deployments (portal, PowerShell, or Bicep) reference a specific image version by ID
quiz.why: Azure Compute Gallery (formerly Shared Image Gallery) is the versioning and distribution layer for your golden images: each build becomes a new image version under an image definition, can be replicated to the regions where you deploy session hosts, and is referenced by ID when you provision new hosts — giving you rollback and staged-rollout capability that a single unversioned managed image doesn't.

quiz.q: When would you choose an ephemeral OS disk over a managed OS disk for a pooled, non-persistent session host?
options: When you want lower storage cost and faster VM reimage/redeploy for non-persistent pooled hosts, accepting that the OS disk is stored on the host's local VM cache/temp storage and is lost on deallocation
Never — ephemeral disks are not supported for AVD session hosts
When the session host needs to retain user profile data on the OS disk between reboots
Only for personal host pools, never for pooled host pools
quiz.why: Ephemeral OS disks are created on the local VM storage (cache or temp disk) instead of remote managed disk storage, which reduces cost and speeds up reimaging — a natural fit for non-persistent pooled session hosts that are expected to be stateless and disposable. Because the disk doesn't persist independently of the VM, it's the wrong choice whenever you need the OS disk to survive deallocation or hold persistent state, which is why personal host pools and any host expected to retain local state typically use managed disks instead.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, explain what Azure Image Builder automates in the golden-image workflow and why a platform team would prefer it over a manual 'build a VM, install apps, sysprep, capture' process.
quiz.answer: Azure Image Builder (AIB) automates the golden-image pipeline end to end: given a base image, a set of customization steps (PowerShell scripts, Windows Update, restart handling, app installers) and a distribution target, it provisions a temporary build VM, applies the customizations, and publishes the resulting image as a new version directly into Azure Compute Gallery — without an engineer manually creating a VM, RDPing in, installing software, and running sysprep by hand. A platform team prefers this because the build becomes a repeatable, source-controlled, auditable definition (an ARM/Bicep template) that can be re-run on a schedule or triggered by a pipeline, which is essential once you're maintaining monthly image refreshes across many host pools rather than a single manually-built image.
quiz.why: AIB turns image building from a manual, error-prone, one-off task into a repeatable automated pipeline that integrates with Azure Compute Gallery versioning — the difference between an image process that scales to dozens of host pools and one that doesn't.

body_markdown:
## Two Decisions That Shape Everything Else

Once your networking is sorted, the two decisions that most determine session host cost, performance, and manageability are: what VM SKU you size for each workload class, and what image that VM boots from. Get sizing wrong and users complain about lag no amount of RDP Shortpath tuning will fix. Get the image process wrong and every patch cycle becomes a manual, error-prone slog across dozens or hundreds of hosts. This lesson covers both properly.

## Sizing Session Hosts by Workload Class

There is no single "right" VM size for AVD — sizing is a function of **workload class** and **density** (sessions per host for pooled pools):

- **Light / task workers**: data entry, basic office apps, a handful of browser tabs. These tolerate higher density — more concurrent sessions per vCPU — and do well on general-purpose burstable or standard VM SKUs with modest vCPU-to-user ratios.
- **Medium / knowledge workers**: full Office suite, multiple browser tabs, occasional video calls, moderate multitasking. This is the most common profile and needs a meaningfully lower sessions-per-vCPU ratio than light workers to keep the experience responsive.
- **Heavy / power users and engineers**: CAD, development workloads, data analysis, sustained video conferencing, multiple high-resolution monitors. These often need dedicated or near-dedicated vCPU allocation per user, more memory per session, and sometimes a GPU-enabled SKU (covered from the vendor-neutral angle in Module 2, and revisited for AVD specifically as NV-series VMs when a workload needs hardware-accelerated graphics).

The practical workflow: start from Microsoft's published workload-class sizing guidance as a baseline, translate that into a target sessions-per-host number for pooled pools, and then **validate against a real pilot group** doing real work before you commit to the SKU for the full fleet. Disk IOPS and throughput matter as much as vCPU and memory — an undersized managed disk can bottleneck a session host that otherwise has plenty of compute headroom, especially during a FSLogix profile load or a boot storm at 9am.

## Choosing the OS: Windows 11 Enterprise Multi-Session

For **pooled** host pools, **Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session** is the default choice: it's licensed and engineered to let several users run independent, concurrent interactive sessions on one VM, which is exactly what makes pooled compute cost-efficient. For **personal** host pools, where each VM is dedicated to a single user, a standard single-session edition of Windows 11 Enterprise is the more common choice, since there's no need for the multi-session capability when nobody is sharing the machine. Either way, the licensing prerequisite is the same family of eligible Microsoft 365 or Windows per-user entitlements you'll cover in Module 4's identity lesson.

## The Golden Image Workflow

A **golden image** is a single, tested VM image — OS plus applications, agents, and baseline configuration — that every session host in a pool (or family of pools) boots from. The alternative — configuring each host by hand after deployment — doesn't scale past a handful of machines and guarantees configuration drift. The golden image workflow looks like this:

1. **Build**: start from a supported base (a Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session marketplace image is the common starting point), install and configure your applications, apply baseline settings, and install the AVD agent components.
2. **Generalize**: run Sysprep (or let your automation tooling handle it) to remove machine-specific identifiers so the image can be deployed to many VMs.
3. **Capture**: publish the generalized image as a managed image or, preferably, directly as a new version in an **Azure Compute Gallery** image definition.
4. **Deploy**: point host pool session host provisioning (portal, PowerShell, or Bicep) at that specific image version.
5. **Refresh**: on a regular cadence, repeat the process, publish a new image version, and roll it out to new or replaced session hosts — this is where the deployment automation and session host update mechanisms from the next lesson come in.

## Azure Compute Gallery: Versioning and Distribution

**Azure Compute Gallery** (the current name for what was previously called Shared Image Gallery) is the layer that turns a one-off captured image into a manageable artifact. Each build becomes a new **image version** under an **image definition**, and Azure Compute Gallery lets you:

- **Replicate** a version to every Azure region where you deploy session hosts, so provisioning pulls the image from a nearby region instead of across the world.
- **Reference a specific version by ID** in your deployment automation, so you can pin a host pool to a known-good version, stage a new version to a validation host pool first, and roll it out to production deliberately rather than accidentally deploying "whatever the latest build happens to be."
- **Share** image definitions across subscriptions in the same tenant (or beyond, with the right RBAC), useful when a central platform team builds images consumed by multiple business-unit subscriptions.

This versioning discipline is what makes a **rollback** possible: if a new image version causes problems, you point deployments back at the prior known-good version instead of trying to hot-fix hosts that are already running.

## Automating the Build with Azure Image Builder

**Azure Image Builder (AIB)** automates the build-generalize-capture sequence itself. You define a template — base image, a list of customizers (PowerShell/shell scripts, Windows Update, restart handling, app installers), and a distribution target (typically an Azure Compute Gallery image definition) — and AIB provisions a temporary build VM, applies the customizations, captures the result, and publishes it as a new gallery version, then tears down the temporary VM. Because the template is just an ARM/Bicep resource, the entire image-build process becomes source-controlled and repeatable through a pipeline, rather than a manual "build a VM, RDP in, install everything, sysprep by hand" exercise that different engineers might do slightly differently each month. AIB also automatically applies **Trusted Launch** settings when the target image definition is configured to support it, keeping security posture consistent without an extra manual step.

## Trusted Launch and Disk Type

Two more decisions round out the session host build:

- **Trusted Launch** combines **Secure Boot** and a **virtual TPM (vTPM)** to protect against boot-level and kernel-level attacks (rootkits, bootkits, malicious code injection into Windows kernel-mode processes) and enables **Credential Guard**. AVD supports provisioning Trusted Launch VMs from custom images stored in Azure Compute Gallery, and it should be treated as a default-on baseline for new session host deployments rather than an optional extra, given there's no meaningful downside for typical AVD workloads.
- **Ephemeral vs. managed OS disks**: an ephemeral OS disk is created on the VM's own local (cache or temp) storage instead of remote managed disk storage. That makes reimaging faster and removes the managed-disk storage cost, which fits **non-persistent pooled session hosts** well — they're meant to be stateless and disposable, and losing the OS disk on deallocation is a non-issue since a fresh copy of the golden image is exactly what you want on the next boot. **Managed OS disks** remain the right choice for personal host pools or any host where the OS disk needs to persist independently of the VM lifecycle.

Put together, sizing and image strategy determine whether your AVD estate is fast and maintainable or a constant source of tickets — and both feed directly into the deployment automation you'll build in the next lesson.

slides.sub: Sizing, building, and versioning the VM users actually land on
slides.narration: Two decisions shape everything about how your session hosts perform and how easy they are to maintain: how you size the virtual machine, and how you build and version the image it boots from. In this lesson we cover sizing by workload class, choosing the right Windows edition, the golden image workflow, versioning through Azure Compute Gallery, automating builds with Azure Image Builder, and the Trusted Launch and disk type decisions that round out the build.

slides.title: Sizing by Workload Class
bullets: Light task workers tolerate higher session density
Medium knowledge workers need a lower sessions-per-vCPU ratio
Heavy power users often need near-dedicated vCPU, sometimes GPU
Disk IOPS matters as much as vCPU and memory
slides.narration: There's no single right VM size for AVD. Light task workers doing data entry tolerate high session density on modest hardware. Medium knowledge workers running the full Office suite and video calls need a meaningfully lower sessions-per-vCPU ratio to stay responsive. Heavy power users, engineers, and designers often need close to dedicated compute per user, and sometimes a GPU-enabled SKU. And don't forget disk IOPS — an undersized disk can bottleneck a host with plenty of spare compute, especially during a profile load or a morning boot storm.

slides.title: Sizing Workflow
bullets: Start from Microsoft's workload-class sizing guidance
Translate into a target sessions-per-host for pooled pools
Validate against a real pilot group doing real work
Only then commit to the fleet-wide SKU
slides.narration: The practical sizing workflow starts with Microsoft's published workload-class guidance as a baseline, translates that into a target number of sessions per host for a pooled pool, and then validates that target against a real pilot group actually doing their day-to-day work before committing to the SKU for the entire fleet. Skipping the pilot step is how organizations end up re-sizing hundreds of hosts six months after go-live.

slides.title: Windows 11 Enterprise Multi-Session
bullets: Lets several users share one VM's OS instance concurrently
The default choice for pooled host pools
Personal host pools typically use single-session editions
Licensing ties to eligible Microsoft 365 or Windows entitlements
slides.narration: Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session is licensed and engineered specifically so multiple users can run independent, concurrent sessions on one virtual machine — that's what makes pooled compute cost-efficient, and it's the default OS choice for pooled host pools. Personal host pools, where each VM belongs to exactly one user, typically use a standard single-session edition instead, since there's no sharing to support. Either edition draws on the same family of eligible Microsoft 365 or Windows per-user licenses.

slides.title: The Golden Image Workflow
bullets: Build once: OS, apps, agents, baseline configuration
Generalize with Sysprep to remove machine-specific identifiers
Capture as a new Azure Compute Gallery image version
Deploy hosts from that version, and refresh on a cadence
slides.narration: A golden image is built once, tested once, and rolled out consistently rather than configured host by host. Build the image with your OS, applications, agents, and baseline configuration in place. Generalize it with Sysprep to strip machine-specific identifiers. Capture the result as a new version in an Azure Compute Gallery image definition. Then deploy new session hosts from that specific version, and repeat the whole cycle on a regular refresh cadence.

slides.title: Azure Compute Gallery
bullets: Stores and versions your golden image as image versions
Replicates versions to every region you deploy into
Deployments reference a specific version by ID
Enables staged rollout and rollback to a known-good version
slides.narration: Azure Compute Gallery is the versioning and distribution layer for your golden images. Every build becomes a new image version under an image definition. You can replicate a version to every region where you deploy session hosts, and your deployment automation references a specific version by ID, which means you can stage a new version to a validation host pool first, then roll it out deliberately, and roll back to a known-good version if something goes wrong.

slides.title: Automating with Azure Image Builder
bullets: Defines base image, customizers, and a distribution target
Provisions a temporary build VM and captures the result
Publishes directly into Azure Compute Gallery
Turns the build into a repeatable, source-controlled pipeline
slides.narration: Azure Image Builder automates the whole build-generalize-capture sequence. You define a template with a base image, a list of customization steps like scripts and Windows Update, and a distribution target, and AIB provisions a temporary build VM, applies the customizations, captures the image, and publishes it directly as a new Azure Compute Gallery version. Because the template is just an ARM or Bicep resource, the entire image process becomes repeatable and source-controlled instead of a manual process different engineers do slightly differently.

slides.title: Trusted Launch
bullets: Combines Secure Boot and a virtual TPM
Protects against rootkits, bootkits, and kernel code injection
Enables Credential Guard
Supported with custom images in Azure Compute Gallery
slides.narration: Trusted Launch combines Secure Boot and a virtual TPM to protect the boot chain and the kernel against rootkits, bootkits, and malicious code injection, and it enables Credential Guard on top. Azure Virtual Desktop supports provisioning Trusted Launch virtual machines from custom images stored in Azure Compute Gallery, and given there's no meaningful downside for typical AVD workloads, treat it as a default-on baseline rather than an optional extra.

slides.title: Ephemeral vs Managed OS Disks
bullets: Ephemeral disks live on local VM cache or temp storage
Faster reimage, lower cost, but lost on deallocation
Good fit for stateless, non-persistent pooled hosts
Managed disks remain right for personal host pools
slides.narration: An ephemeral OS disk is created on the session host's own local storage instead of remote managed disk storage, which speeds up reimaging and removes managed disk cost. Because non-persistent pooled hosts are meant to be stateless and disposable anyway, losing the disk on deallocation isn't a problem — a fresh golden image is exactly what you want on the next boot. Personal host pools, where the OS disk needs to persist with the VM, stay on managed disks.

slides.title: Bringing Sizing and Images Together
bullets: Sizing and image strategy jointly determine host performance
Both feed directly into the deployment automation ahead
A pilot-validated SKU plus a versioned image is the baseline
Get this right before scaling out session hosts
slides.narration: Sizing and image strategy together determine whether your session hosts are fast and maintainable or a constant source of tickets. A pilot-validated VM size paired with a properly versioned golden image is the baseline every production AVD environment should start from, and both of these decisions feed directly into the deployment automation we build in the next lesson.
